title: Babylon falls (Revelation 17–18)
hook: the merchants weep over a city that trafficked in bodies and souls

segments.voice: Yesterday, a song by a sea of glass, the song of Moses and the Lamb. Your line was great and marvelous. What did you praise out loud? Day one thousand three hundred eight.

A shipping manifest. That's what sits in the middle of Revelation eighteen, and it reads like one. Gold, silver, precious stones, pearls. Fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet. Ivory, bronze, iron, marble. Cinnamon, incense, ointments, frankincense. Wine, oil, fine flour, wheat. Cattle, sheep, horses, chariots. And then, at the very end of the list, two more items of cargo. The merchants who bought and sold all of it are standing at a distance, watching a great city burn, and weeping. And the reason the text gives for their tears: nobody is buying their goods anymore. Today's word is that city's end: Babylon falls.

First, the city. In chapter seventeen Babylon is pictured as a woman dressed in purple and scarlet, riding a beast, drunk on the blood of the saints. Babylon had once carried the people of Jerusalem into exile, and in Revelation the name becomes a code. Some readers hear Rome, the city of seven hills; others hear any great city or empire that grows rich by using people up. Second, the cry. An angel shouts: "Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen." Then the mourners: "Alas, alas that great city Babylon, that mighty city! for in one hour is thy judgment come." Kings mourn, merchants mourn, sailors mourn. Everyone who profited mourns. Third, the end of the list. The King James closes the cargo with these words: "and slaves, and souls of men." The Greek word behind slaves there is the word for bodies. Bodies, and human souls, listed right after the horses and chariots, as if they were the same kind of thing. Some readers hear that as the heart of the charge against Babylon: it put people on the inventory. Fourth, the call. Before the fire, a voice from heaven says: "Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins." Christians have heard that call in different ways: some as leaving a place, some as refusing to live by its rules while still inside it. Some readers say Babylon is never far away: in the clothes, the phones, the food, wherever a price is low because someone, somewhere, was treated like cargo.

Here's the practice: plan to buy something fairly traded. Settle, and breathe. Look at what's around you right now. Your shirt. Your coffee. The phone in your hand. Pick one thing and wonder, without guilt, whose hands touched it before yours. Then choose one thing you'll buy this week, and decide to find a version made by people who were paid and treated fairly. Coffee, chocolate, a T-shirt. If you pray, you can pray for the people whose hands made your things. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Babylon falls. In Revelation seventeen and eighteen, the great trading city collapses in one hour, and its cargo list ends with bodies and human souls.
Your line: bodies and souls. Today, buy one thing fairly traded, or swap one purchase for a fairer one, and remember the people behind it. Day one thousand three hundred eight.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Revelation 18 as a call to look at how goods are made and traded, and churches and Christian groups run fair-trade stalls and campaigns against human trafficking.

fork.setup: you're a merchant who grew rich trading with the great city. now you watch it burn from a distance. what do you do?
options: rush in to save the people.
stand far off and weep for your lost trade.
celebrate that the city is gone.
fork.reveal: the merchants stand afar off, weeping, because no one buys their goods anymore. the list of what they sold ends with human beings.

original.note: Greek: body. in Revelation 18:13 the plural, bodies, is the word the King James renders slaves.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient city destroyed for being wicked.
what it means: a city that put people on its cargo list, and the call to come out of her.
what a scholar hears: the Greek reads bodies, and souls of men, at the end of the list; Babylon, the city of Israel's exile, becomes a code for empire.

notes: Hook's cargo list follows Revelation 18:12–13 in the KJV, slightly shortened (e.g., 'odours' given as incense, 'thyine wood' and 'beasts' left out). Confirm it reads as a summary.
Claim: the Greek behind KJV 'slaves' in 18:13 is σωμάτων, 'bodies' (the KJV margin also gives 'bodies'). Confirm.
Readings of Babylon: Rome (17:9, seven mountains) or any exploiting city or empire, given as 'some readers' / 'others'. Babylon's role in Israel's exile is biblical (2 Kings 25). Confirm.
Two readings of 'come out of her' (leaving, or refusing its ways from inside) given without ranking.
Practice suggests fair-trade buying; no brand or certification named.
Editor pass: 'carried Israel into exile' made 'the people of Jerusalem' (Judah); 'the charge against Babylon' framed as some readers' reading.

Audit 2026-10-02: 'not because of the fire' overstated (18:9, 18:15 also name the burning and her torment); now gives 18:11's reason only. Closing 'Babylon is in your clothes' moved from narrator claim to 'some readers say'; stock 'ordinary Tuesday' cut.
